Introduction:
Brazil, was severely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, reporting >38 million cases and 700 000 deaths [ 1 , 2 ]. Since the first case on 23 February 2020, extensive research has examined the seroprevalence [ 3–5 ], adherence to protection measures [ 6 ], excess mortality [ 7 ], transmission routes [ 8 ], averted cases [ 9 , 10 ], risk assessment [ 11 , 12 ], and vaccine effectiveness [ 13 ]. Despite these findings, comprehensive population-based data on case history and hospitalization across demographic and socioeconomic groups remain scarce [ 14 , 15 ].

In 2020, the EPICOVID survey—a multistage nationwide study—provided insights into the COVID-19 prevalence, mask use, and infection risk [ 3 , 4 , 6 , 16 , 17 ]. Here, we introduce the EPICOVID 2.0 survey and examine the distribution of self-reported COVID-19 cases and hospitalizations across the Brazilian population, considering factors such as sex, age, region, skin colour/ethnicity, comorbidities, schooling, and socioeconomic status.
Methods:
### Study design and sampling

EPICOVID 2.0 was a nationwide survey encompassing all Brazilian states and the Federal District. The Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) divides the country into 133 intermediate regions and the survey included the urban area of the most populous city within each region ( Figure 1 and Supplementary Material 1 ) [ 18 ].

The survey employed a multistage probabilistic sampling method in which, within each city, 25 census tracts—small geographic areas used to collect census data—were selected with a probability proportionate to population size. Ten households were randomly chosen from each census tract by using maps and household listings provided by IBGE, resulting in 250 households per city. The survey was conducted between March and June 2024 with the Brazilian Ministry of Health’s support.

We randomly defined a starting point in each census tract to select the first 10 households. To select other households within the same census tract, we adopted a systematic skip of 10 households. During the visit, the study team recorded the ages and genders of all household members. One household member was randomly selected to participate. If the selected person refused, then we selected a second person. If the person declined, then the study team proceeded to the next household on the right. If the household consisted of only one person and this person refused, then the study team proceeded to the next household. Our projected sample size was 33 250 individuals.

Written informed consent was obtained from all adult participants and minor participants’ parents or legal guardians.

### Data collection and analysis

A smartphone app was used for data collection by following a computer-assisted personal interview protocol. The questionnaire (provided in Supplementary Material 2 ) consisted of 215 questions divided into four sections: (i) general/socio-demographics (age, gender, skin colour/ethnicity, education, occupation, and household assets), (ii) COVID-19 symptoms and post-COVID-19 clinical manifestations, (iii) COVID-19 impacts on participant’s life, and (iv) COVID-19 vaccination history. Our analysis focuses on the questionnaire’s first and second sections. Respondents were asked whether they had had COVID-19 (Yes, No, Don’t know/Ignored) and, if so, the number of episodes, the date (month and year), the diagnostic method (Polymerase chain reaction [PCR], rapid test at the pharmacy, rapid test performed at home, diagnosis given by a doctor, don’t know/ignored) of each episode, whether hospitalized, and, if so, for how long.

The characteristics of participants were categorized by: sex (Male, Female), age in years (categorized as 0–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, and ≥80 years), self-reported skin colour/ethnicity [White, Black, Pardo (mixed Black), Asian, Indigenous], region of residency (Northeast, North, Center-West, Southeast, South), Wealth Index (quintile-based, described in Supplementary Material 3 ), and schooling (≤4, 5–8, 9–12, and ≥13 years of education).

First, we used Poisson regression models to estimate the crude and adjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) between the covariates and reporting at least one COVID-19 episode. This model is suitable for analysing count data and estimating PRs directly, which is preferable to odds ratios when the outcome is common (as is COVID-19 in our study). Furthermore, to examine how overlapping social identities influenced the COVID-19 outcomes, we performed an intersectionality analysis. The intersectionality analysis was operationalized through the inclusion of all product terms among race, sex, and socioeconomic status in our survey-weighted Poisson regression models to estimate the PRs for prior COVID-19 by using the most-privileged group (i.e. wealthier White males) as the reference. This approach provides a nuanced understanding of how multiple forms of marginalization contributed to disparities in the COVID-19 outcomes. Lastly, we calculated the odds ratios and 95% CIs through ordinal logistic regression models to assess the factors associated with the number of COVID-19 episodes. This model is appropriate for analysing ordered categorical outcomes and estimates the relative odds of experiencing more COVID-19 episodes relative to one episode. We calculated the sampling weights to represent the target population by using IBGE data, including the population size, sex, age, and race/ethnicity for each city. First, we extracted the population distribution by sex, age, and race/ethnicity from the 2022 census and compared it to that of our sample [ 19 ]. We calculated a weight by dividing the census population distribution by the corresponding population in the sample. Secondly, to account for variations in population sizes across the municipalities, we divided the population of each municipality by the number of interviews conducted. Lastly, we multiplied the demographic and municipal weights to create a single weighting variable. The weighted and unweighted distributions are detailed in Supplementary Material 4 . Later, we defined the survey design, with the city as the stratification variable and the census tract as the primary sampling unit.

To assess how imperfect recall of COVID-19 episodes might have influenced our estimates, we conducted a Monte Carlo-based probabilistic bias analysis for outcome misclassification. We assumed that a respondent’s self-report of ever having had COVID-19 could suffer from both false negatives (i.e. failure to remember a true infection) and false positives (erroneously reporting infection). We sampled the sensitivity and specificity [Se ∼ Beta(80,20), Sp ∼ Beta(95,5)] over 1000 iterations, refitted our survey-weighted Poisson model each time, and reported the PRs and intervals.

All analyses were conducted by using the ‘svy’ command in Stata and ‘survey’ R package, which adjusted for the complex survey design by accounting for stratification, clustering, and within-city correlations. The code is available in Supplementary Material 3 .

### Role of the funding source

The study’s funder had no role in its design, analysis, interpretation, or manuscript writing.
Results:
To achieve the sample size of 33 250, we visited ∼90 000 households, with 92.5% of the selected individuals agreeing to participate. The sample overrepresented individuals from the North region (16.5% versus 8.5%) and underrepresented those from the Southeast (24.8% versus 41.8%). Males were underrepresented (38.0% versus 48.5%). Individuals aged ≤19 years were underrepresented, whereas those aged ≥50 years were overrepresented. Individuals identifying as Asian and Indigenous were overrepresented (1.9% and 1.4% versus 0.4% and 0.6%, respectively), whereas Whites were underrepresented. Most participants were aged ≥40 years (59.7%), with most having 5–8 years (21.6%) and 9–12 years (44.1%) of schooling ( Table 1 ).

Among the participants, 28.6% (95% CI, 27.3–29.9) (i.e. 9320) reported having had COVID-19. The age groups of 40–49 and 50–59 years reported the most diagnoses (1723 and 1744 individuals) ( Table 2 ). Females presented a 1.2 (95% CI, 1.1–1.3) higher prevalence. The Southeast region accounted for 25% (2470) of the COVID-19 cases, followed closely by the Northeast (2369 participants). The North and South regions had the highest weighted prevalence of 35.1% and 33.5%, respectively. Adjusted (by age and sex) PRs, with the Northeast region as a reference, were the highest for the Center-West (1.6, 95% CI, 1.1–2.2) and the Southeast (1.5, 95% CI, 1.1–2.2). Adjusted PRs revealed a marginally lower prevalence for Black (0.8, 95% CI, 0.7–0.9) and Pardo participants (0.9, 95% CI, 0.8–0.9) compared with Whites. Higher education levels and wealth were positively associated with having had COVID-19. Among those with COVID-19, 4978 had at least one comorbidity, with hypertension being the most common ( n = 3253). Higher prevalence and PRs were observed for participants with thrombosis (36.7, 95% CI, 27.9–46.5) and diabetes (34.4, 95% CI, 31.1–37.9) ( Table 2 ).

Among those who had experienced COVID-19, 596 (4.5%, 95% CI, 3.8–5.2) were hospitalized, with an average length of stay of 10.4 days. Most of those who were hospitalized were >40 years old (on average 52 years), females ( n = 371), residing in the Northeast region ( n = 168), and self-declared Pardos ( n = 292), with most having between 9 and 12 years ( n = 239) of schooling and reporting one COVID-19 episode ( n = 474). Individuals with multiple COVID-19 episodes were 3.7 times (95% CI, 1.5–8.8) more likely to be hospitalized. Further, most hospitalized participants had hypertension ( n = 307) or diabetes ( n = 200), and those with kidney (4.1, 95% CI, 1.1–15.4) or heart (3.9, 95% CI, 1.3–11.2) chronic disease presented higher PRs compared with participants without comorbidity ( Table 3 ).

The estimates of COVID-19 PRs between combinations of sex, skin colour/ethnicity, and wealth are shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary Table S5 ( Supplementary Material 3 ). When compared with White males in the wealthiest quintile, Pardo , Black, and Indigenous males in the poorest quintiles presented significantly lower PRs. In general, females presented higher PRs than their male counterparts. Nevertheless, only Pardo females in the poorest wealth quintile presented a significantly lower PR (0.6, 95% CI, 0.5–0.7).

Figure 3 and Supplementary Table S6 ( Supplementary Material 3 ) show the PRs of hospitalization between combinations of skin colour/ethnicity and wealth. The Indigenous in the wealthier quintile (4.7, 95% CI, 1.1–2.0) and Pardos (1.9, 95% CI, 1.1–3.2) in the poorest quintile presented a higher PR.

A total of 7234 participants reported a single COVID-19 episode, 1586 reported two episodes, and 408 reported three episodes. Table 4 presents the crude odds ratio (OR) associated with the number of COVID-19 episodes. When compared with individuals aged 0–19 years, the age groups ranging from 20–29 to 50–59 years were more likely to present more COVID-19 episodes, while Asians were less likely to report a higher number of COVID-19 cases (0.4, 95% CI, 0.2–0.9). The wealthiest (5th quintile) had higher odds of reporting more COVID-19 episodes (1.4, 95% CI, 1.0–2.0). Lastly, participants with asthma/bronchitis (1.7, 95% CI, 1.0–2.8) and chronic kidney disease (1.7, 95% CI, 1.0–2.7) had a higher OR compared with individuals without comorbidity.

The sensitivity analysis ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 in Supplementary Material 3 ) produced PRs that were similar to our primary estimates: e.g. participants with ≥13 years of schooling had a PR of 1.9 [95% simulation interval (SI) 1.4–2.1] versus 1.8 (95% CI, 1.4–2.1) in the main analysis and the highest wealth quintile presented a PR of 1.7 (95% SI, 1.4–2.0) compared with 1.9 (95% CI, 1.6–2.2), indicating that recall misclassification had a minimal impact on our findings.
Discussion:
To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the largest studies to have examined the impacts of COVID-19 in low- and middle-income countries. It highlights the regional disparities in the COVID-19 burden in Brazil, with the North and South regions experiencing the most significant impact of the disease, while the Center-West and Southeast regions present the highest PRs. Moreover, our findings suggest an association between COVID-19 and both wealth quintiles and higher educational attainment—a proxy for higher socioeconomic status (see Supplementary Table S1 in Supplementary Material 3 ). Additionally, individuals with multiple COVID-19 episodes were more prone to being hospitalized and comorbidities were associated with COVID-19 cases, multiple episodes, and hospitalizations.

Our overall prevalence is similar to that observed in other Brazilian studies. The Covitel, a nationwide telephone survey, found a 25.5% prevalence of self-reported COVID-19 [ 20 ]. Nevertheless, serological surveys, such as the previous EPICOVID and COmVIDa, reported a higher prevalence [ 3–5 ]. Serologic studies capture infections more effectively than self-reported surveys, which are subject to recall bias and underreporting.

In contrast to the previous EPICOVID [ 3 , 4 ], our study observed a higher prevalence among women, consistently with studies from China, the USA, and England, in which females presented higher SARS-CoV-2 prevalence, but males presented a higher probability of hospitalization and death [ 21–26 ].

In our study, among the country’s regions, we found that living in the Center-West was strongly associated with COVID-19. Several studies have reported disproportionately high rates of hospitalizations and mortality in the North and Center-West regions of Brazil. Consequently, the highest decline in life expectancy in Brazil occurred in Center-West states (18%–47%) [ 7 , 10 , 27–30 ]. Additionally, the Center-West region presented the lowest vaccination proportion (81.33%, 95% CI, 78.54–83.83; Supplementary Table S2 ).

Interestingly, we found no significant differences in COVID-19 or hospitalization among races/ethnicities. While this may appear to counter previous findings, it likely reflects disparities in testing and healthcare access rather than a true absence of disparities in outcomes. Prior studies have shown that Black, mixed Black, and Indigenous populations face higher COVID-19 case prevalence, mortality, and in-hospital mortality, mainly driven by socioeconomic and healthcare inequalities. For instance, Baqui et al. reported higher mortality among hospitalized Black and Pardo Brazilians (1.4 and 1.3, respectively) [ 27 ] and Hallal et al. observed higher seroprevalence among Indigenous people (6.4%) due to increased exposure risks [ 4 ]. These findings and those of other studies [ 30–33 ] emphasize that systemic inequities, not ethnicity, often shape COVID-19 outcomes. Our findings underscore the limitations of marginalized groups’ access to testing and healthcare. Lower socioeconomic status often intersects with race and ethnicity, potentially restricting timely testing and accurate reporting. Thus, while we observed no statistical differences, these results may mask underlying health inequities that must be addressed through equitable healthcare and testing access.

Higher education and wealth were associated with higher COVID-19 prevalence and reinfections. The positive relationship between COVID-19 and both years of schooling and wealth may reflect disparities in healthcare access. Individuals with more formal education may have been more likely to access testing and healthcare services. Furthermore, a statistical difference was observed between vaccination, schooling, and wealth, with higher coverage ratios of vaccinated individuals in the wealthier quintiles and higher educational attainment groups (see Silveira MF et al. , in the same IJE supplement). The Covitel study also observed a higher prevalence in participants who had higher educational attainment, with those with ≥12 years of education presenting a 2.5-fold higher chance of contracting COVID-19 [ 20 ]. A previous Brazilian study using COVID-19 National Household Sample Survey data reported a positive association between income and the likelihood of COVID-19 testing [ 34 ]. Similar patterns were observed in the USA, China, and Switzerland. Individuals residing in areas with higher socioeconomic status or higher incomes were more likely to undergo SARS-CoV-2 testing. They had higher infection rates, but required fewer hospitalizations and ICU (Intensive Care Unit) admissions, and experienced lower mortality rates [ 24 , 25 , 35–40 ]. Conversely, a study in the USA found a positive correlation between areas with a lower proportion of uninsured individuals and higher testing and case frequency [ 21 ].

Higher hospitalization risk among individuals with multiple COVID-19 infections could be attributed to several factors, including cumulative health impacts, reduced immunity, and pre-existing conditions. They may present certain risk factors (e.g. comorbidities or compromised immunity) that increase the susceptibility to reinfection and worsen outcomes upon reinfection. Chronic health conditions, common among high-risk groups, could also worsen each successive COVID-19 infection, leading to more reinfection and hospitalizations. Comorbidities partially explained this increased prevalence when accounting for assessed conditions (i.e. diabetes, hypertension, asthma, bronchitis, cancer, and kidney, heart, or vascular chronic disease) ( Supplementary Tables S3 and S4 in Supplementary Material 3 ). Individuals with COVID-19 reinfections may face variants that evade acquired immunity from past infections or vaccinations, resulting in more severe cases [ 21 , 41–47 ].

The increase in the reported incidence of COVID-19 in the wealthier population may be partly due to recall bias, with wealthier individuals being more likely to remember past episodes. It may also be a consequence of broader structural determinants of health, particularly access to healthcare and diagnostic services. Lower-income populations are more likely to experience barriers to healthcare access, including delays in seeking care, testing, and obtaining diagnoses. In contrast, reported hospital admission rates, which are likely to be less prone to recall bias, did not show a clear socioeconomic pattern, so that, even if the incidence was higher among the wealthy, other reasons may have contributed to increased severity among the poor and led to hospitalization. These may include greater vulnerability due to undernutrition and the presence of comorbidity. These findings align with global research emphasizing the role of social determinants in shaping COVID-19 outcomes, reinforcing the need for policies to reduce health inequities through improved healthcare access, economic support, and housing interventions [ 4 , 16 , 27–29 ]. In contrast, in settings with equitable access to testing, such as the UK, different patterns of socioeconomic status infection risk underscore how differential access to testing and care may shape observed inequalities in COVID-19 outcomes [ 48 ]. We believe that, in our study, wealthier participants were more likely to access testing and medical attention when symptomatic, or even asymptomatic, through screening, leading to higher case ascertainment. In contrast, poorer households faced greater barriers to testing, resulting in the underdetection of infections despite equal or higher true incidence, as well as in increased severity.

At a global scale, high-income countries have demonstrated superior capacity for contact tracing, testing, and outbreak response, along with more robust clinical services, compared with lower-income countries [ 26 , 49 ]. Hart’s inverse care law proposed that ‘the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served’ [ 50 ].

It is important to consider the limitations of this study when interpreting the findings. Our sample was restricted to cities that constitute regional hubs and are generally larger, more developed, and have better healthcare infrastructure than smaller cities, especially rural communities. Consequently, our study does not capture the experience of rural populations, which comprise ∼15% of Brazilians [ 19 ]. Recall bias is a concern, as participants reflected on experiences from ≤4 years prior, which may have impacted accuracy, especially for mild infections. Moreover, the potential access to testing was likely differential across socioeconomic status. To mitigate this, we included contextual cues in the questionnaire and encouraged participants to consult personal records to provide the dates when possible. Our sample comprises only survey respondents who were alive at the time of the interview. Individuals who died after a COVID-19 episode, particularly older adults, are thus excluded, introducing survivorship bias, which may have attenuated the observed associations with age. Additionally, our sample included fewer younger individuals (≤19 years), Whites, and males when compared with the overall population, which was expected given the study design and was taken into account during the analysis. The underrepresentation of Whites may stem from lower response rates in apartment buildings and gated communities, where many White individuals reside [ 4 , 17 , 51 ]. The lower representation of younger individuals and men could have been due to data collection occurring during school hours for the younger and working hours for men, who are more likely to be employed outside the home [ 52 , 53 ]. We could not gather dates for one-third (36.9%) of the COVID-19 cases reported ( n = 3548), limiting our ability to explore the variant effects on reinfections. The dynamics of the pandemic in Brazil were heavily influenced by the emergence of variants of concern and vaccination rollout, which varied over time. For example, the Gamma variant, which dominated in early 2021, was associated with higher hospitalization rates, while the Omicron variant, which emerged in late 2021, led to a surge in cases, but lower severity. Without precise infection timing, we cannot evaluate these influences on our findings [ 4 , 5 , 7 , 10 , 11 , 13 ].

Lastly, our study may be prone to some bias associated with access to testing/diagnosis; consequently, the prevalence may be underestimated. As mentioned above, barriers to testing can be related to region, wealth, and schooling. Due to the lack of information on testing for individuals without a history of COVID-19 diagnosis, direct assessment of the association between access to testing and socioeconomic variables, such as wealth quintiles and years of schooling, was not feasible. Despite the biases and limitations that we have outlined, our probabilistic bias analysis showed that plausible levels of under‐recall minimally impacted the key PR estimates, suggesting the robustness of our core findings.

In conclusion, this study highlights the regional disparities in the COVID-19 burden in Brazil and how socioeconomic factors affected its prevalence. Higher educational attainment correlates with increased reporting of infections, likely due to healthcare access and testing disparities. These findings emphasize the need for targeted public health strategies to address these disparities and ensure equitable healthcare access across different populations. Future research should involve diverse samples, especially from rural areas, to better understand the pandemic’s impact on all Brazilians.
